notes:
I've gathered enough to write notes, but the coverage has gaps. My searches and page reads ran out before I could reach Gill, Ellicott, any Reformed, Lutheran or Orthodox site, the NET Bible or Bible Odyssey. So the notes rest mainly on David Guzik (Enduring Word), Precept Austin, Coffman (StudyLight), the Pulpit Commentary and Clarke (from search excerpts), and Catholic Answers. Verses 12–14 are thin as a result.

**v. 1**
- "Burden" (Hebrew *massa'*) comes from a verb meaning to lift or carry. Here it means a weighty word full of meaning. The Hebrew literally says "by the hand of Malachi," and the Greek Old Testament reads "by the hand of his messenger." https://www.preceptaustin.org/malachi_1_commentary
- The message goes to the whole nation, not just the northern or southern kingdom. The people who returned from Babylon came from all the tribes. https://www.preceptaustin.org/malachi_1_commentary
- Setting: about 100 years after the return from exile, in or just after Nehemiah's time. The temple was rebuilt, there was a "governor" (v. 8), and the same sins appear as in Nehemiah 13: corrupt priests, mixed marriages and withheld tithes. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-1/
- Coffman points out that the burden is addressed *to* Israel, not *against* it. He also defends Malachi as the prophet's real name. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/malachi-1.html

**v. 2**
- God assures Israel of His love before He corrects them. G. Campbell Morgan renders it "I have loved you, I do love you, I will love you." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-1/
- Morgan also notes that when people stop loving God, they start wondering whether God loves them. https://www.preceptaustin.org/malachi_1_commentary
- "How have You loved us?" is the first of seven questions the people put to God in the book. Guzik says these questions reveal doubting, discouraged hearts. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-1/
- A different view: Coffman says the verse doesn't promise lasting love to Israel as an ethnic nation. He applies it to "spiritual Israel," the faithful remnant. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/malachi-1.html

**vv. 2–3 (Jacob loved, Esau hated): the main debated text**
- Guzik: God points Israel to His choice of them as the proof of His love. "Hated" doesn't mean God cursed Esau, who was a blessed man (Genesis 33). It means Esau was left unchosen for Abraham's blessing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-1/
- Guzik cites Leon Morris, who agrees with Calvin that the sense is "accepted" and "rejected." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-1/
- Guzik sets out both positions, conditional election (based on foreknowledge) and unconditional election, and judges that Jacob's election here was unconditional. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-1/
- Guzik also quotes Deane (Pulpit Commentary): Malachi isn't teaching double predestination but comparing the histories of two nations. Both sinned; Israel was restored by mercy and Edom was not. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-1/
- Guzik notes that Spurgeon is often quoted as saying the real puzzle is not why God hated Esau but why He loved Jacob. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-1/
- Coffman (Churches of Christ) says the choice concerned nations, not individuals, and says nothing about eternal destiny. God's foreknowledge would have given Him a righteous basis for choosing. Citing Keil, he rejects softening "hate" to "love less" here, because Edom's ruin is the proof given. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/malachi-1.html
- I couldn't reach any Reformed (Ligonier, Desiring God), Wesleyan or Lutheran treatment of this verse, so I can't report their positions from their own teachers.

**v. 3**
- Babylon conquered both Israel and Edom, but only Israel was restored. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-1/
- Coffman says the exact devastation of Edom Malachi refers to is unknown, but it was evidently recent. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/malachi-1.html

**v. 4**
- Edom's status as "unchosen" won't change. Guzik reads this as comfort: once God chose Israel, they stayed chosen. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-1/
- Coffman compares Edom's boast to Isaiah 9:10. He also says "LORD of Hosts" means God rules all hosts: armies, angels and stars. Citing Keil, he says Edom never recovered, especially from Maccabean times onward, and he notes the Herods were Idumaeans (descendants of Edom). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/malachi-1.html

**v. 5**
- Coffman: God is shown great beyond Israel through His judgments and fulfilled prophecies. He rejects the scholarly view that the prophet expected the Messianic age within his hearers' lifetime. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/malachi-1.html

**v. 6**
- The priests called God Father and Master but didn't honor Him. Their surprised question shows they slid into contempt gradually, without noticing. Guzik applies this to today's ministers and quotes Richard Baxter. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-1/
- Coffman sees an appeal to the Fifth Commandment, and compares the priests' claim of innocence to Matthew 7:22–23. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/malachi-1.html

**v. 7**
- "Food" (or "bread") means the altar sacrifices (Leviticus 21:6), and "table" means the altar. Coffman ties it to the Lord's Table in the New Testament. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/malachi-1.html
- Guzik applies "defiled food" to sermons that lack God's word, are carelessly prepared, or have no passion. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-1/

**v. 8**
- Blemished offerings were forbidden (Leviticus 22:20–23; Deuteronomy 15:21). People offered God what the governor wouldn't accept, unlike David, who refused to offer what cost him nothing (2 Samuel 24:24). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-1/
- Coffman says "governor" means a Persian-style official, and warns against building the book's date on this verse. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/malachi-1.html

**v. 9**
- Guzik reads the verse as rich with irony. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-1/
- Coffman notes that some Jewish and other commentators take it as a sincere call to repent, but prefers the ironic reading. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/malachi-1.html

**v. 10**
- Not everything that is offered to God as worship is accepted by God as worship. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-1/
- Coffman links the verse to Hosea 3:4 (Israel "without sacrifice") and to the temple's destruction in AD 70. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/malachi-1.html

**v. 11 (a pure offering among the nations): the most debated verse**
- Guzik: if Israel won't worship rightly, God will find worshippers among the Gentiles. Jesus' command to spread the Gospel and to go to every nation is part of God's way of fulfilling this promise. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide2017-Mal/Mal-1.cfm
- Pulpit Commentary: God doesn't need the priests' maimed sacrifices, because pure worship will come from every nation. The Fathers and mediaeval writers, and many modern commentators, see in this verse a prophecy of the Holy Eucharist. https://biblehub.com/malachi/1-11.htm
- Bible Hub's own notes: incense stands for prayer, and the "pure offerings" are fulfilled in Christ's sacrifice and in believers' spiritual sacrifices (1 Peter 2:5). https://biblehub.com/malachi/1-11.htm
- Methodist: Adam Clarke says the verse foretells the total abolition of the Mosaic sacrifices, and the establishment of a *spiritual* worship over the whole earth. He names the incense of praise and the offering of the spotless Lamb. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/malachi/1-11.html
- Coffman: the only pure offering is Christ's blood, honored at the Lord's Supper every Sunday. He thinks some Roman Catholic writers went too far. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/malachi/1-11.html
- Catholic: Catholic Answers quotes the historian J. N. D. Kelly, who says early Christians seized upon Malachi 1:10–11 as a prophecy of the Eucharist. It also cites the Didache, Justin Martyr and Irenaeus. https://www.catholic.com/tract/the-sacrifice-of-the-mass
- GotQuestions (Evangelical) confirms that One biblical passage the Catholic Church cites in support of the Eucharist as a sacrifice is Malachi 1:10–11. https://www.gotquestions.org/Holy-Eucharist.html
- Another reading: some say the verse means pagan worship in Malachi's own day was already acceptable to God. I only found it as Coffman's target: he calls the claim that pagans offered "pure offerings" indefensible. He didn't name who holds it, and I didn't read the scholars themselves. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/malachi-1.html

**vv. 12–13**
- Guzik: their selfish, insincere worship left the worshippers themselves unsatisfied. True worship is never **contemptible** or **a weariness**. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide2017-Mal/Mal-1.cfm
- I didn't find any further verse-level comment on these two verses.

**v. 14**
- Guzik compares the deceiver to Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5): pretending to give everything while holding back. They didn't treat God as the great King He is. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-1/

**What I couldn't find:** Gill, Ellicott, Reformed, Lutheran or Orthodox sources; the NET Bible notes or Bible Odyssey; and any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace use of this chapter. A second round of searching would be needed to fill those in, especially Reformed and Wesleyan readings of vv. 2–3.
